title: Approval and accountability
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: What do your kids, your team or you need more of: approval, or accountability?

A student said that he always has a way of making one work harder, whether his kids or his employees. Jose said: he makes you want to be better. He is an incredible leader. He is really empowering people.
What is it that someone does when they empower you, Jose asked? A student said: they tell you to keep going and try harder. Jose said the word he was looking for is accountability.

He is all about accountability, Jose said. If you look at the goals he sets, he takes on the responsibility. The danger of leadership without accountability is that you don't have goals and you are not tracking specific, measurable results day to day.

Number two in his team building, Jose said: he looks at the strengths and weaknesses of everybody on his team. He has an incredible intuition. When he meets somebody, he understands their skill set immediately. And he nurtures relationships all the time. He is a long-term player. That is why people are so loyal to him.
Jose spoke about a scene where the author drove his child in an open jeep and the child froze. I did that for you, the author said. I was working on making you tough.

For those of us who are parents, Jose said, we need to show our children that life is tough. You want to show love to your kids, but at the same time you want to make them a little tough. You want accountability there. What you don't want is the child who victimizes themselves.
You don't hear him saying: oh my God, poor me, I'm being bullied by a bigger company. Victimizing yourself comes from a negative belief system, he said. It comes from a lack of approval.

There is a real delicate balance between approval and accountability, Jose said. Those are the two magic words. His father gave approval only once or twice, but it was enough to give him the security to say: I'm not a victim. I look at everything as a challenge.

A student added that some of the other children were spoiled and not thick-skinned, and he did not want his children like that. Jose agreed: if you spoil your kids, and they know a lot of wealth is coming, it affects their work ethic. You take away the struggle, the grit, the habits.

Without the struggle, Jose said, you will not accomplish your goals, and you will not have the internal value every human needs: I approve of myself. I accomplished many things I set my mind to do. That affects your identity.
He mentioned a novel called Less Than Zero, about very wealthy young people with no purpose, who become adrenaline junkies because that is all that is left.
Where do you need more approval, and where more accountability?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write one person you lead or raise.
Write what approval they get from you, and what accountability.
Write where you victimize yourself: a blame you tell about a bigger player.
Write one challenge you will help them meet head on.
Write one struggle you will not take away from them.

check.q: What did Jose say are the two magic words?
What did Jose say victimizing yourself comes from?
choices: A negative belief system and a lack of approval

check.q: What did Jose say happens if you take away the struggle from your children?
choices: It affects their work ethic and identity

recap: Balance approval with accountability. Don't take away the struggle.
